title: What Working With Agents Is Like for Educators Who Don't Know
author: Mike Caulfield
summary: Mike Caulfield narrates a short session with an AI agent to show educators what current AI work actually looks like, arguing that many people discussing education and AI hold a 2024 picture of the technology. Using his project of rating thousands of presidential-administration events for significance and controversy, he asks the agent to fix a misleading chart midpoint, accepts some of its suggestions, and adds a correction of his own about unequal event counts across administrations. The five minutes shown are part of a longer evening process in which the agent also finds gaps in his data and redesigns a data structure around an upload limit. His central argument is that this work does not reduce critical thinking but demands more of it, since every result prompts new questions about method, bias and categories. He concludes that agents turn thinking into viewable results while shrinking execution effort, and that educators should get up to speed because a classroom using such tools would not have to explain why critical thinking matters.
points: Caulfield argues that much public discussion of AI in education rests on a 2024 model of chatbots that answer questions, far from what practitioners do with agents.
In his example, a five-minute exchange with an agent corrected a chart, surfaced a statistical flaw, and led him to add his own insight about skewed event counts.
The statistical and methodological questions the work raises, from presentist bias to categorisation, undercut the claim that agents simply cause cognitive offloading.
Agents make the results of a line of thinking visible almost immediately, which in turn prompts more critical thinking.
He urges educators to get up to speed soon, since a classroom with such tools creates a natural demand for critical thinking.
quotes: There are an awful lot of people out there talking about education and AI that have a 2024 understanding of what AI is and it would be to the benefit of the public if they read something that confused them.
What I just showed you above is 5 minutes of interaction with an agent. It’s a process. An evening session involves a lot of this.

Even this understates the nature of working with these systems. While I was working on the problem above it was going out and finding gaps in my event lists, searching for other public records (beside the executive action logs) that might be productive lead generation for finding missed events.

Now, if you are looking at this analysis and you have a million statistical objections and questions, I have to ask you, do you feel less cognitively engaged with statistics than during an average hour of an average day or less?
Many people’s model of AI until now has been you ask a question and get an answer.

To formulate a question well is to formulate a research plan and to be able to look at the results of that plan almost instantly and discuss it. Agents are a tool that turn critical thinking into viewable results, which in turn prompt more critical thinking, and they do that by massively shrinking the amount of execution effort that must be expended to follow a line of though to its conclusions.

A tool that makes the results of its user’s critical thinking visible or apparent is a tool that creates a demand for critical thinking, and a classroom that harnesses such a tool is one that won’t have to explain to students why critical thinking matters.
But if this stuff is unfamiliar to you and you are in the business of thinking through the future of education, you should get up to speed as soon as possible.
